entrada.texto:
Peer-to-Peer Networking and Applications (2025) 18:302
2.2.1 Blockchain types
Blockchains are commonly categorized into public, private, 
consortium, and hybrid types. Each offers distinct trade-offs 
in decentralization, performance, and access control. Table 
3 summarizes their key characteristics and suitability for 
sensitive data sharing scenarios.
As shown in Table 3, public blockchains prioritize decen-
tralization and transparency but suffer from scalability 
issues. In contrast, private and consortium blockchains offer 
better performance and privacy but at the cost of decentral-
ization. Hybrid blockchains attempt to balance these trade-
offs, though their implementation remains complex.
2.2.2 Consensus protocol
Consensus protocols determine how blockchain networks 
achieve agreement on the next block. While various mecha-
nisms exist, Proof of Work (PoW), Proof of Stake (PoS), 
and Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance (PBFT) are among 
the most widely used. Table 4 compares their key character-
istics, strengths, and limitations.
As shown in Table 4, each consensus mechanism pres -
ents unique trade-offs relevant to healthcare data sharing. 
handling both unstructured data (e.g., clinical notes, images) 
and structured data (e.g., lab results, diagnoses) in ways that 
maintain patient privacy and comply with regulatory stan -
dards [71].
Data transfer refers to the secure transmission of health-
care data between different systems, institutions, or stake -
holders, such as research institutions, regulatory agencies, 
and healthcare providers [ 72]. Since these systems may 
adhere to various standards and protocols, robust security 
measures are essential to protect sensitive data during tran -
sit [ 73]. Techniques such as Proxy Re-Encryption (PRE) 
and Transport Layer Security (TLS) help ensure that data is 
not intercepted, tampered with, or exposed during transmis-
sion, thereby upholding privacy standards and compliance 
with regulatory frameworks [57].
2.2 Blockchain
Blockchain is a decentralized ledger that ensures secure, 
transparent, and immutable transactions across distributed 
networks. Its key features–decentralization, immutability, 
and cryptographic security–make it particularly appealing 
for healthcare data sharing, where patient privacy and data 
integrity are paramount.

resposta.resumo: O trecho classifica blockchains em públicos, privados, consórcios e híbridos, apontando trade‑offs entre descentralização, desempenho e controle de acesso. Descreve ainda os principais protocolos de consenso (PoW, PoS, PBFT) e suas implicações para privacidade e escalabilidade em compartilhamento de dados de saúde. Menciona técnicas de transferência segura, como Proxy Re‑Encryption (PRE) e TLS, essenciais para proteger dados sensíveis em ambientes distribuídos.

possibilidades: Avaliar blockchains híbridos como camada de integração entre dispositivos IoT edge e back‑ends de saúde em smart cities, mitigando a complexidade de implementação.
Projetar um mecanismo de consenso leve (ex.: PBFT adaptado) para redes de sensores urbanos, equilibrando latência e resistência a falhas bizantinas.
Desenvolver um módulo de busca criptograficamente segura usando Proxy Re‑Encryption (PRE) para consultas sobre dados de saúde armazenados em blockchains.
Criar políticas de controle de acesso baseadas em atributos (ABE) acopladas a credenciais verificáveis (SSI) para autorizar dispositivos edge em cenários de interoperabilidade inter‑organizacional.
